slides: Now we go deep into the content rubric.
And we'll start with relevance to the task, and the central idea.
So first, two terms.
Relevance to the task is the link between what we write, and the issue the task is about.
The central idea is how clear our arguments are, how logically they connect to each other, and how well they explain our position.
Here's a common problem.
Students don't state their position in the opening paragraph, like we recommend.
And then one paragraph is for the cameras, the next one is against the cameras... and the reader doesn't get what you want anymore. For? Against?
Now, it's fine to discuss the issue from a few angles, for and against, and to deal with the opposing view.
But before anything else, the reader has to understand what you want from him.
It's really, really important to read the task. And to read it carefully.
I don't skim the background. I actually give it time. We'll have a whole lesson on analysing the task later.
The task has two parts. The background text, and the discussion question at the end.
Pay attention to everything there. Hints, important words, ideas for arguments.
And above all, answer the discussion question. The line in bold at the end.
Let's take the example we already know. Face-recognition cameras in public spaces.
The first part is the background text. Think of it as a teaser.
A teaser says, come, let me show you what you're about to read. So the background tells us what the essay is going to be about.
Then comes the discussion question. And that's the actual issue.
So why did I say teaser? Because the background often has ideas for arguments in it.
Look here. Supporters claim the system will reduce crime and security incidents.
Now, some students are afraid to take ideas from here. They say, no, I need to show creativity, I want to come up with arguments myself.
Coming up with arguments yourself is fine. But the background is there to help you start writing.
So the message is, take what's here and build an essay from it. But getting an idea for an argument doesn't mean you now get a six.
You still have to take the idea, develop it, and support it.
And why is the background there at all? Well, when there was only a short background, a lot of students drifted completely away from the issue.
That's why tasks come with a fuller background. It gives context, and it points you toward what to write about.
Actually, they could have asked us only the question.
In your opinion, should security authorities be allowed to install face-recognition cameras in public spaces? Give reasons.
I could write an essay on that alone. But the background helps. It gives directions, where to start, and roughly what they want us to discuss.
So read the background, analyse it, and mark the important words that will help you later.
Since we know this task, let's just look at some possible opening positions.
In my opinion, they should be allowed. That's my opinion. Of course I'll need to explain why. But it's fine.
In my opinion, they should not be allowed. Also fine. And again, I'll have to explain why.
In my opinion, they should be allowed, but only under certain conditions.
A lot of students are afraid of this one. They asked yes or no, didn't they? So is it yes, or no?

It's fine. It's called a complex position. Yes, with a clear limit. Yes, no, or yes-with-conditions... all three answer the question. We'll talk about choosing between them in the lesson on choosing a position.
Now look at this last sentence.
In my opinion, security authorities can be trusted to do their job ethically and not to misuse face-recognition cameras.
Nobody asked whether they'll do it ethically. This sentence misses the discussion question. The relevance is very weak.
Yes, it's the same topic. And it could lead to a fair argument. Maybe the people watching the cameras will leak the database.
Maybe they'll follow people they know, their neighbours. Maybe that really could happen. It's a fair concern.
But they didn't ask us whether security people are ethical. They asked whether to allow the cameras.
Now, in the complex position, I can use it. Like, I understand that some security staff may abuse their access, so I suggest limits to prevent it, or reduce it.
But as a position, this sentence doesn't answer the question.
Relevance isn't only about your position.
During the essay you also bring arguments. So make sure they clearly support your position.
The arguments in the body of the essay are called key sentences. Each argument paragraph starts with one.
And after each key sentence, we explain it. Why we think our argument, our key sentence, is true.
Now, the central idea.
It's how clear the arguments in your essay are. Whoever reads them understands what you want to say. They connect logically, and they support your position.
The official guide says it clearly. The central idea must be clearly worded, and every other idea and argument in the essay must relate to it.
That's the line of the whole essay. Opening paragraph, argument one, argument two, and so on.
But the central idea isn't only the line of the whole essay.
Inside every paragraph there's a line too. The development of my key sentence has to be in a logical order.
The development is made of steps. Links, like mini-arguments. A leads to B, B leads to C, C leads to D... and here I am, at the result I wanted.
And that's exactly the chain. The cause-and-effect steps we plan before writing. It gets its own lesson later.
So where does all this show up in the rubric?
The central idea shows up in three criteria. Development, focus and coherence, and critical thinking.
Relevance shows up mainly in development. I make sure my arguments really relate to what I was asked.
Focus and coherence fit the central idea more. And critical thinking covers everything.
So now we understand, more or less, what they want from the content. Next, the criteria one by one. See you in the next lesson.
